title: In 16 homogenised DOISST v2.1 versions (60S-60N, 1982-2025), heatwave-day, frequency and record-year results survive; the flat peak-intensity trend and cold-spell lengthening do not
abstract: Question: NOAA Daily OISST v2.1 (DOISST) has steps in fast variance and in the mean at input changes. Earlier studies corrected each with one choice. Which published marine heatwave (MHW) and cold-spell (MCS) results stay true for all reasonable corrections? Approach: we built 16 versions of DOISST: four mean corrections (step fields fitted on HadSST4.2 or ERSSTv5, no ship term, or half the correction) times four noise targets (sub-32-day spectrum of 1985-2006, 2007-2015, 2016-2020 or 2021-2025). We computed 17 statistics (Hobday definitions, 1983-2012 baseline) on 29,129 ice-free one-degree cells (60S-60N, 1982-2025), tested 29 published global results and 176 regional trends, and checked the mean correction at 142 moored buoys. Results: at the buoys, published DOISST drifts +0.034 C per decade, the full corrections -0.02 and the half correction +0.007, so the mean correction is uncertain by a factor of two. The rise of MHW days (published +21.2, ensemble +13.5 to +22.2 days per decade), MHW frequency and category II+ days, the doubling of 99th-percentile days (1982-2016), the fall of MCS days, the 2023 record year and the 489-day 2023-2024 daily record streak survive. The MHW duration trend keeps its sign but is too large (+4.45 against +1.53 to +4.21). Published DOISST shows almost no MHW peak-intensity trend (+0.006 C per decade) and a negative tropical trend; all members give +0.046 to +0.054 and a positive tropical trend, and make 2023 the peak-intensity record year (published rank 7). The published MCS duration rise (+0.75) becomes -0.24 to +0.03, and no member shows weaker cold spells. The noise target, not the mean correction, sets 72% of the MHW-day spread and 96% of the duration spread. Limitations: the members are plausible choices, not a probability distribution; buoys are DOISST inputs; we compare with our own run of each published statistic.
